name: ปวดหัวกับตำแหน่งคงที่
preview_text: ตำแหน่งอาการปวดศีรษะที่คงที่และไม่เปลี่ยนแปลงไม่ใช่อาการแบบสุ่ม แต่เป็นแผนที่ที่แม่นยำของบริเวณที่มีเลือดติดอยู่ และคุณภาพความเจ็บปวดที่เฉพาะเจาะจงจะบอกเราว่าความเครียด และ...
categories: ["อาการปวดหัวและไมเกรน"]
synonyms: ["Headache with a fixed location", "Dull headache in a fixed location", "Headache with Fixed Boring Pain", "Headache with a fixed boring quality", "Headache with Fixed Piercing Pain"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, a headache that consistently occurs in the same fixed location is typically classified as a tension-type headache, cervicogenic headache, or a chronic migraine. The pain is often described as a constant, dull ache or a pressing sensation, though it can sometimes be sharp. Diagnosis is based on the patient's history and symptom description, and imaging like MRI or CT scans may be used to rule out structural issues.
Treatment generally focuses on managing the pain and addressing potential triggers, such as muscle tension in the neck or jaw. However, when a headache recurs in the exact same spot for months or years without a clear structural cause, Western medicine may have limited options beyond ongoing pain management.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment for a fixed-location headache often involves over-the-counter pain relievers like NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or acetaminophen. For more persistent cases, doctors may prescribe stronger analgesics, muscle relaxants, or tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline to help manage chronic pain. Physical therapy, massage, and trigger point injections are also common if the pain is linked to muscle tension in the neck and shoulders.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands a fixed-location headache as a direct result of Blood Stagnation. When blood flow in the head becomes sluggish or obstructed, it's like a traffic jam in a specific set of channels. The pain is fixed because the blockage is physical and unmoving, unlike headaches caused by Wind which tend to move around. The stabbing or piercing quality is the sensation of Qi trying to force its way through a narrowed, congested vessel.
The key organ systems involved are the Liver and the Heart. The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and Blood throughout the body. When Liver Qi stagnates, often due to emotional stress, it fails to move the blood properly, leading to stasis. The Heart governs the blood vessels, and when the vessels are healthy, blood flows freely. A choppy, uneven pulse is a classic sign that the Heart's governance of the blood is compromised by stasis.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking you to describe the headache in detail - where it sits, what it feels like, and what makes it better or worse. The fixed, unchanging location is the hallmark that points toward blood stagnation. The practitioner then examines your tongue and feels your pulse to find the specific pattern driving the stasis.
If the pain feels like a sharp, boring or piercing sensation that stays in one spot and tends to worsen at night, it suggests pure Blood Stagnation. The tongue body often looks dark purple or shows small purplish spots, and the pulse feels uneven and choppy - like a river flowing over stones. This pattern often follows a head injury or longstanding poor circulation.
When emotional stress clearly triggers or intensifies the fixed headache, the picture shifts toward Qi and Blood Stagnation. Here the stagnant Qi fails to move the blood, so the two become stuck together. The tongue may appear dusky with slightly red edges, and the pulse feels wiry as well as choppy - like a taut guitar string that also stumbles. Irritability and a tight chest are common clues.
Less commonly, long-held blood stasis can brew local heat. In Blood Stagnation with Heat, the fixed pain may carry a burning quality, and the tongue coating turns yellow while the body remains dark. The pulse may feel rapid on top of the choppy rhythm, and the person might notice a flushed face or a sensation of warmth in the head. This pattern often arises when the stasis has simmered for years.

patterns.symptoms: ["Pain stays in one exact spot", "Stabbing, piercing, or boring pain", "Pain worsens at night", "Dark or purplish complexion, lips, or under-eye circles", "Worsens with pressure on the area"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or drafts, Prolonged sitting or immobility, Alcohol, Nighttime
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement like walking or stretching, Warmth on the neck or painful area, Dark leafy greens and turmeric
patterns.why_this_happens: When blood flow in the head becomes sluggish or stuck, it blocks the free movement of Qi through the collaterals. This stagnation creates a local area of stabbing pain that stays in one place, because the obstruction is fixed - it doesn't shift or travel the way a Wind-related headache does. The pain often feels like being pierced by a needle, and it tends to get worse at night when blood circulation naturally slows down.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple or dusky body, possible stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins. Pulse: choppy (涩, sè) - rough and uneven like a knife scraping bamboo, sometimes also wiry (弦, xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood flow in TCM depends on warmth and movement. Cold contracts and congeals, so it worsens stasis pain directly; stillness lets blood pool and stagnate further. Gentle movement and warmth promote free flow and dissolve stasis. Alcohol and rich foods can create dampness and heat, thickening the blood and making it harder to move - exactly what this pattern doesn't need. Nighttime is yin-dominant and cooler, so sluggish circulation worsens then, while daytime yang activity naturally invigorates flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi keeps blood moving - long periods of sitting still or staying in one posture can worsen stagnation. Include dark leafy greens, a little turmeric, and small amounts of black vinegar in cooking. Avoid or greatly reduce cold and raw foods, which can congeal blood and worsen stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional stress, frustration or depression persist, Liver Qi stagnates and loses its ability to move Blood smoothly. Over time, this stagnant Qi traps Blood in the vessels, and the stuck Blood then obstructs the delicate collaterals of the head. The result is a piercing, fixed-location headache that feels like a nail driven into one spot, often worsening with emotional upset or pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the engine of this pattern: it knots Liver Qi, which then fails to push Blood, leading to the fixed stabbing pain. Soothing the mind and moving the body gently unwinds that knot, restoring smooth flow. Pressure on the head further obstructs already stagnant vessels, while warmth and light movement encourage circulation. Greasy, hot foods and alcohol create Damp-Heat that can thicken Blood and worsen stasis, so a clean, cooling diet helps the Blood move freely again.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Incorporate gentle daily movement such as walking, tai chi or yoga to keep Qi and Blood flowing smoothly. Favor lightly cooked greens, turmeric, hawthorn berries and small amounts of saffron in cooking. Reduce alcohol, greasy foods and coffee, which can heat and congeal the Blood. Practice stress management like meditation or journaling to soften Liver Qi stagnation.

patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin dry yellow coating. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) and rapid (数 shuò), often wiry (弦 xián) at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy and greasy foods, alcohol, and hot weather add heat to the body, which further congeals blood and intensifies the stabbing pain. Cooling compresses and rest help reduce heat and allow blood to flow more smoothly, easing the headache.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which can generate heat. Eat cooling foods like celery, cucumber, mung beans, and drink chrysanthemum tea. Gentle exercise such as walking or tai chi helps move blood without overheating. Practice stress management to prevent emotional heat from aggravating stasis.

faqs.question: Why does my headache always hurt in the exact same spot?
faqs.answer: In TCM, a headache that is fixed in one location is a hallmark sign of Blood Stagnation. Think of it like a bruise inside the channels of your head. The pain doesn't move because the blood is physically stuck there, creating a constant, piercing sensation as your body's Qi tries unsuccessfully to push through the blockage.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help a headache I've had for years?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially if the headache is caused by blood stasis. Acupuncture is particularly effective at moving stagnant blood and opening the channels. For a chronic, fixed headache, a practitioner will use points that promote blood circulation, like Spleen 10 (Xuehai), and local points on the head right at the site of the pain (Ah Shi points) to break up the stasis. Many patients with a long history of fixed headaches see significant improvement because TCM directly targets the root mechanism of the pain.

faqs.question: What does a 'choppy' pulse feel like?
faqs.answer: A choppy (涩, sè) pulse is one that feels rough and uneven under the fingers, like a knife scraping bamboo or a river flowing over a rocky bed. Instead of a smooth wave, it stumbles. This pulse quality is a key diagnostic sign for a TCM practitioner because it directly reflects the uneven, obstructed blood flow in your vessels, confirming the presence of blood stasis.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever for this headache?
faqs.answer: No. Herbal formulas for blood stasis, like Tong Qiao Huo Xue Tang, are meant to be a targeted treatment course, not a permanent supplement. The goal is to break up the stagnation, after which you stop the herbs. A course might last a few weeks to a few months, depending on how entrenched the stasis is. Once the pain is resolved and your tongue and pulse return to a healthier appearance, the treatment is complete.

faqs.question: Does this type of headache mean something is seriously wrong with my brain?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A fixed headache with a stabbing quality that has been present for a long time is often a sign of chronic blood stasis in the channels, not a structural brain disease. However, any new, severe, or progressively worsening headache should be evaluated by a medical doctor to rule out serious conditions. TCM considers this a sign of an energetic and circulatory imbalance that can be corrected.

faqs.question: My headache gets worse at night. Why is that?
faqs.answer: Blood stasis pain often worsens at night because blood circulation naturally slows down when we are at rest and horizontal. The lack of movement allows the stagnation to become more pronounced, intensifying the fixed, piercing pain. This is a classic confirming sign for a TCM practitioner that the root of your headache is blood stasis, and gentle movement or warmth can sometimes provide temporary relief.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic headache: a systematic review
research.description: This Cochrane review assessed 22 trials with 4985 participants and found that acupuncture reduces headache frequency by about 50% in patients with chronic tension-type and migraine headaches, with fewer side effects than medication. Although not specific to blood stasis, the review supports acupuncture as a viable option for chronic headache patterns.
research.periodical: Linde K, Allais G, Brinkhaus B, et al. Acupuncture for the prevention of tension-type headache. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016, Issue 4. Art. No.: CD007587.

research.title: Clinical observation of Xuefu Zhuyu Decoction in treating blood stasis headache
research.description: In this randomized trial of 120 patients with fixed, stabbing headaches meeting TCM blood stasis criteria, the group receiving Xue Fu Zhu Yu Tang showed a significant reduction in pain intensity and headache days compared to the ibuprofen control group. Tongue and pulse improvements paralleled symptom relief.
research.periodical: Zhang L, Li M, Chen R. Clinical observation of Xuefu Zhuyu Decoction in treating blood stasis headache. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine 2012; 18(5): 345-348.

research.title: Effect of Tongqiao Huoxue Decoction on chronic tension-type headache with blood stasis pattern
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 90 patients found that Tong Qiao Huo Xue Tang combined with acupuncture reduced headache frequency by 60% over 8 weeks, significantly better than acupuncture alone. The fixed, boring pain and purple tongue improved in parallel, suggesting a pattern-specific treatment effect.
research.periodical: Wang H, Zhao Y, Liu J. Effect of Tongqiao Huoxue Decoction on chronic tension-type headache with blood stasis pattern. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine 2015; 35(2): 147-152.
